meta.purpose: Ground-truth side of the oracle premise test (V3_PLAN.md §5, step 1).
meta.selectionRule:
INCLUSION. An artwork enters the evaluation set when the warehouse holds at least one palette for it
that (a) was graded `strong` — the era's top absolute grade and the only one the legacy distillation
exports as an endorsement — and (b) still has `strong` as its standing grade under the recency rule,
i.e. no later comparison graded that exact palette `weak-fallback` or `unacceptable`. The artwork's
gradient ground truth is that palette's `gradient` boolean: a gradient decision a human looked at and
accepted.

EXCLUSIONS, each counted in meta.counts:
  - `acceptable` grades. Explicitly not endorsements (PHASE_0_DECISIONS.md §5). A not-rejected
    palette is not an accepted gradient decision.
  - Reviewer corrections (`correctionsKind: endorsed-sample`). They carry role hexes only; the v2-3
    warehouse records no gradient boolean on a correction, so they contribute no ground truth here.
  - Records whose image cannot be resolved to a file on disk (no batch entry, no cached result).
  - Records whose stored content hash disagrees with the file now on disk (the palette was graded
    against different bytes; the label does not transfer).
  - Artworks the inference runtime cannot decode (checked separately by the runner's preflight, not
    here) — recorded, never silently dropped.

CONFLICTS. Two levels, both resolved the same way and both flagged:
  1. Same artwork, same exact palette, graded more than once: the legacy distillation's recency rule
     verbatim — latest recordedAt wins. A palette whose standing grade is bad never enters.
  2. Same artwork, DIFFERENT accepted palettes disagreeing on the gradient boolean: this is not a
     contradiction in the warehouse — several palettes can be valid for one artwork, and v2-3's own
     gradient neutrality work shows both a flat and a gradient palette can be acceptable for the same
     cover. The recency rule is extended to it (latest accepted observation wins) so the set has a
     defensible single label per artwork, and the artwork is marked `conflicted: true` with its full
     observation history. Report agreement both including and excluding these; if they are a material
     share of any disagreement, that is a finding about the ground truth, not about the oracle.
     An exact timestamp tie between disagreeing observations is `underdetermined` and is excluded
     from the primary set (kept in the file, `included: false`).
meta.recencyRule: Latest-timestamped grade wins (reviewer decision 2026-08-02). Where the same artwork and the same exact palette were graded more than once, the most recent grade is the pair's standing verdict; earlier grades are history, not live contradictions. Only conflicting grades sharing an identical timestamp stay unresolved, and those warn rather than block.
meta.groundTruthEpistemology: An ACCEPTED ALGORITHM DECISION, not an elicited human label. The reviewer graded palettes, not artworks; `strong` was awarded to the preferred side of a blinded pair (or to both sides on an `equal` answer). The gradient boolean is one field of a palette the reviewer accepted as a whole, so the reviewer's attention was on the palette, not necessarily on that flag. `strong` also does not mean unique-best: several palettes can be valid for one artwork, and the same palette was sometimes graded differently in different comparisons. Treat disagreement with the oracle as a prompt to look at the artwork, never as a proof that the oracle is wrong.
meta.renditionScoping: Ground truth is scoped to the exact rendition the reviewer saw. Run the oracle on `image.absolutePath` and nothing else. Where two entries share `artworkId`, they are two renditions of one artwork: aggregate per artworkId before quoting an agreement rate (pipeline doc §7.2).

crossCheckAgainstLegacyDistillation.note: Both sides apply the same grade filter and the same recency rule, so the two sets must match. A non-zero difference means one of the two drifted and must be investigated before the run.

observations.notes: This one is genuinely hard because the artwork is basically one big blue-to-white gradient, and so in that case we cannot really use a background to surface gradient to imitate it. Otherwise, there is for sure going to be some points in the gradient where the foreground cannot be distinguished from the background. So even though the artwork is very strongly a gradient, this is a rare case where we have to go flat. You can even see a case that should be forbidden, which is that the foreground and the background have the same color in option A's palette (or at least not visually distinguishable). This should give an APCA contrast of 0, which is strictly forbidden between foreground and background

This artwork is an exception, because

because of its limited "range" of hues, using a gradient as a background guarantees that both colors are used in the background (white and blue) and that the foreground colors (foreground and accent) will be almost impossible to distinguish in *at least some parts* of the gradient.

Follow-up on the calibration-2 strong ({bg #000102, surface #380703, fg #d50306, accent #7e0202}, all reds): 'could also have been nice with a Slate #706c6d accent, so it's not full red'. An alternative sample, not a downgrade — the all-red palette stays strong. Evidence for a mild hue-diversity preference on the accent when fg already carries the identity hue (adjacent to the skap one-hue-one-direction principle: the two reds are one direction; a neutral accent diversifies without stealing identity).

Sharpening the Slate-accent sample: 'in this case Slate #706c6d almost acts as a true *accent* since the entire palette is red.' Principle: accent-ness is CONTEXTUAL to the palette, not absolute — the accent role is what stands apart from the palette's dominant hue field. In a monochromatic (all-red) palette a neutral is the true accent; in a neutral-heavy palette a chromatic color is. Current machinery scores accent chroma/identity absolutely; it has no notion of within-palette distinctiveness as the accent's job.
